title: Your brain can’t stop reading, so ‘red’ in blue ink trips you up
body: Show someone the word red printed in blue ink and ask for the ink colour, and they take significantly longer than when word and colour agree. John Ridley Stroop published the effect in English in 1935, though Erich Rudolf Jaensch had reported it in German in 1929. The leading explanations agree on one thing: **reading is automatic**. The brain reads a word faster than it recognises a colour, so the word’s answer arrives first and has to be suppressed, and naming a colour simply demands more attention. The clash is now a standard clinical test.

slides.alt: Two columns of colour words. On the left each word is printed in its own colour; on the right each word is printed in a clashing colour. The instruction reads: say the ink colour, not the word.
slides.caption: Try naming the ink colours out loud. The right column is slower.

slides.heading: Why it is hard: three theories
items: Speed: the brain reads words faster than it recognises colours
Attention: naming a colour takes more attention than encoding a word
Pathway strength: reading is the better-practised route, so it wins

slides.heading: A tool in the clinic
slides.text: Stroop interference increases with brain damage and in disorders such as schizophrenia, addictions and depression. In the emotional Stroop, depressed people are slower to name the colour of negative words than of neutral ones. Reaction times on the task fall steadily from early childhood to early adulthood.

slides.question: Who first published the effect, in German, in 1929?
slides.explanation: Jaensch published it in 1929; Stroop’s 1935 English paper made it famous. Its roots go back to the work of Cattell and Wundt.
